abstracts.value: We develop a constructive framework for characterizing modulated symmetries and their gauging in $d$-dimensional lattice systems. The modulation profiles are organized as a finite-dimensional representation of the space group acting on a finite Abelian internal symmetry group. Since the corresponding automorphism group is finite, the nontrivial spatial action factors through a finite quotient of the space group, leading to periodic modulation patterns and providing a classification framework for discrete Abelian modulated symmetries. The symmetry-allowed local interactions are systematically obtained from a kernel construction, which also yields an algebra of open operators. Upon gauging, its elements are transmuted into extended Wilson and boundary operators while retaining their algebraic relations. In the deconfined regime, the resulting algebra realizes a mixed 't Hooft anomaly, providing a microscopic route to Abelian crystalline symmetry-enriched topological phases (SETs). These SETs do not mix electric and magnetic sectors, which transform in mutually contragredient representations, thereby preserving their braiding pairing. We illustrate the framework through explicit examples and show that several models present in the literature fit naturally within our construction.

abstracts.value: Quantum fidelity estimation is a fundamental task in quantum information and computing to benchmark the quality of quantum states, and hence of quantum processes, on noisy quantum hardware. Point estimates of fidelity by existing methods generally lack the rigorous uncertainty quantification required for reliable preparation and verification of these tasks. While Bayesian and bootstrap frameworks are widely used for uncertainty quantification, they are sensitive to model misspecification or lack formal coverage guarantees in non-asymptotic regimes. This paper introduces a hybrid "Bayesian-informed" conformal prediction-based framework to provide distribution-free, rigorous prediction intervals for quantum state fidelity estimation which can be used, with care, to approximate confidence intervals with respect to the quantum randomness of Born's rule. The framework requires a point estimator, and we consider both classical point estimators as well as data-driven neural net estimators. We evaluate the robustness of the methodology across a diverse range of experimental challenges, including finite-sample noise, tomographic incompleteness, physical model error, and out-of-distribution data. Our results demonstrate that conformalized estimators maintain statistical validity where traditional methods fail, offering a scalable and reliable approach for the verification of modern quantum systems. The best performing variant of our methodology is based on a class-conditional conformal prediction, as this most closely approximates the conditional coverage desired for a true confidence interval.

titles.title: Uncertainty Quantification for Quantum Fidelity Estimation

abstracts.value: In this paper, we investigate the quantum behaviour near the classical singularity of a black hole. We describe the black-hole interior by the Kantowski-Sachs metric, with a string propagating in this region. This approach is motivated by the fact that, near the classical singularity, spacetime curvature reaches Planck or string scales, necessitating a description in terms of string-theoretic degrees of freedom. The string dynamics is formulated via the Polyakov action, and the combined system is canonically quantized to derive the corresponding Wheeler-DeWitt equation. Although the equation is separable in the radial and azimuthal string sectors, the remaining geometric and string degrees of freedom are nontrivially coupled. To address this, we employ a perturbative approach and obtain the wave function up to first order. At the zeroth-order, the angular part is described by the general Heun function, while the geometric part is expressed in terms of the Bessel function. The first-order wave function is governed by a source term containing the zeroth-order solution, and we obtain its explicit expression in terms of the complementary function and the particular integral. We confirm regularity of the wave function at both zeroth and first order, at the singularity as well as at the horizon. Regularity at the horizon imposes a discretization condition on one eigenvalue, while another eigenvalue is quantized due to the azimuthal periodicity of the wave function. Importantly, both zeroth- and first-order solutions satisfy the DeWitt boundary condition, implying resolution of the black hole singularity within this quantum framework.

titles.title: Probing the Black Hole Singularity with a Quantum String

abstracts.value: Primordial black holes, whose formation in the early Universe was first hypothesized by Ya.B.~Zel'dovich and I.D.~Novikov in 1966 (the text of this pioneering article is provided in Appendix II to this review), have attracted increasing attention in recent years. This review describes various models of primordial black hole formation, as well as methods for testing these models with astronomical and astrophysical observations. In particular, we discuss in detail the formation of primordial black holes and their clusters through the collapse of closed domain walls and through effects associated with extra spatial dimensions of the Universe.

abstracts.value: Low-loss dielectric films are an important component of superconducting circuits with applications ranging from quantum information to superconducting detectors for astrophysics. In millimeter-wave detector circuits, dielectric loss can be the limiting factor on efficiency and resonator performance. Some advantageous detector fabrication architectures require dielectric deposition at temperatures substantially lower than those conventionally used to achieve low dielectric loss. In this work, we characterize silicon nitride (SiN$_x$) films deposited by inductively coupled plasma chemical vapor deposition (ICPCVD) at $150\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for use in temperature-constrained superconducting detector fabrication. We measure the dielectric loss tangent of these films at $\sim 4-7$ GHz using superconducting niobium microstrip resonators and extract the loss by fitting the temperature-dependent resonant frequency to a two-level-system model. We vary the N$_2$/SiH$_4$ precursor-flow ratio between dielectric depositions and find a clear trend of decreasing loss with decreasing N$_2$/SiH$_4$. We additionally find that applying an RF substrate bias during deposition reduces the loss compared to films deposited without bias. These results identify precursor ratio and substrate bias as practical process parameters for improving low-temperature SiN$_x$ for superconducting detector circuits.

titles.title: Microwave Loss in Low-Temperature ICPCVD Silicon Nitride: Dependence on Precursor Ratio and RF Substrate Bias

abstracts.value: Effective vacuum sectors in modified theories of gravity are often represented by anisotropic stress-energy tensors, even when the underlying source is geometric rather than material. This raises a broader question: can such effective stresses be characterized intrinsically through a covariant constitutive structure, rather than modeled phenomenologically as exotic fluids? We address this question in pseudo-complex general relativity (pcGR), where a constrained variational formulation identifies the effective vacuum source as geometric in origin but does not uniquely determine the corresponding geometric constraint sector. For the static pseudo-complex Schwarzschild solution, we show that the effective vacuum tensor separates naturally into an isotropic contribution and a purely transverse contribution associated with the intrinsic geometry of the two-dimensional subspace orthogonal to the timelike and radial directions. This decomposition leads to a constitutive formulation based on the transverse metric. Its infinitesimal deformations split uniquely into trace and traceless shear modes, with the static solution having only an isotropic transverse response. Within the class of local constitutive variables that depend algebraically on the transverse metric and whose first variation generates the trace projector with stateindependent normalization, the logarithmic transverse area strain is the minimal scalar constitutive coordinate.

titles.title: Constitutive Geometry of the Effective Vacuum Sector of Pseudo-Complex General Relativity

abstracts.value: Asymptotic Safety provides a promising framework for the quantization of Scalar-Tensor theories as non-perturbatively renormalizable quantum field theories. Over the past years, growing evidence has accumulated for the existence of non-trivial renormalization group fixed points in a variety of Scalar-Tensor models. In this work, we investigate the robustness of these fixed points under significant modifications of the computational setup. In particular, we employ a gauge condition that explicitly depends on the dynamical scalar field, going beyond a mere gauge-parameter deformation of the standard linear covariant gauges commonly used in the literature. Exploring different field parameterizations, we identify fixed points belonging to the Gaussian Matter class in four spacetime dimensions that are consistent with previous studies. The real part of the critical exponents associated with the scalar-field mass and the non-minimal scalar-curvature coupling turn out to have very small absolute value. We provide a comprehensive exploration of how the anomalous dimension of the scalar field and field parameterization impact those critical exponents showing that fixed-point candidates with two or four relevant directions emerge.

abstracts.value: Galaxy recession velocities are commonly used to measure the Hubble constant, $H_0$, with peculiar velocities treated as random noise. Around massive clusters, however, these motions can be predicted by the gravitational potential of the central halo, allowing them to be modeled rather than averaged over. Past analyses relied on analytic approximations for the distance-infall-velocity relation, whose accuracy has not been tested using realistic cosmological simulations. We use halos from the IllustrisTNG simulation to quantify the bias and precision of several commonly used Hubble-flow models. We find that widely used fitting functions systematically underestimate $H_0$, whereas the full analytical solution reduces but does not eliminate these biases. We develop a simulation-based method to infer $H_0$ and apply it to TRGB distance samples around the Virgo Cluster. We find $H_0=74.4\pm 2.9$ and $73.4\pm 3.9$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ (stat) for the minor and the major infall models, respectively. Correcting for the bias calibrated on TNG halos, these measurements raise the value of $H_0$ to $81.6 \pm 7.8$ and $87.3 \pm 8.8$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ (stat+sys), where the minor infall model has the smallest bias from the Virgo mocks. We show that statistical errors are dominated by the residual velocity scatter around the infall model, while systematic errors are dominated by the transformation to the structure's comoving frame and halo population variance. These results establish a framework for interpreting cluster infall measurements and explain trends in previous $H_0$ inferences.

titles.title: Debiasing Local Cluster Infall Reveals $\boldsymbol{H_0}$: Application to the Virgo Cluster

abstracts.value: We investigate the relaxation dynamics and steady state of a qubit interacting with a coherent environment through an energy-conserving flip-flop interaction within the Markovian repeated-interaction framework. We derive an exact analytical solution for the evolving and stationary state, nonperturbative in the environmental coherence. We show that environmental coherence provides a resource for dissipative state preparation by expanding the set of accessible steady states. In particular, coherent ancillas can increase the system ground- state population beyond that of the bath, corresponding to an effective temperature below the bath temperature, and enhance its steady-state purity, with these effects controlled by the interplay between the system energy scale and the system-ancilla coupling. Nevertheless, we prove that the purity of the system can never exceed the purity of the ancilla. We further analyze the thermodynamics of the protocol and show that environmental coherence can modify and even reverse the natural direction of heat transfer, giving rise to anomalous heat flow. Remarkably, for fixed interaction parameters, the direction of the coherence-induced heat transfer is governed by the relative phase between the system and ancilla coherence, whereas their magnitudes determine the amount of heat exchanged. Our results establish environmental coherence as a resource for controlling steady-state preparation and energy transfer in repeated-interaction dynamics.

titles.title: Coherence-assisted quantum state preparation and thermal control through repeated interactions

abstracts.value: The conditional colour-magnitude distribution (CCMD) model connects the galaxy colour-luminosity distribution with dark matter halo mass, which has been constrained in Xu et al. by jointly modelling the two-point correlation functions of a large galaxy sample of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) in fine bins of galaxy colour and luminosity. We test the CCMD model of the galaxy-halo connection using counts-in-cells (CIC) statistics by comparing CCMD model predictions with SDSS measurements for 16 subsamples of galaxies in various luminosity and colour bins. In addition, we compare SDSS measurements with three analytic models of CIC distribution. The CCMD model provides a good description of the SDSS CIC measurements for most subsamples. The exceptions are the void probability functions and CIC distributions with cell radius 5 Mpc/h for a few subsamples in the luminous bins, which are not well described by the analytic models, either. For these subsamples, in general, removing the Sloan Great Wall from SDSS or introducing velocity bias to the CCMD model does not resolve the disagreement. Finally, with the help of the CCMD mocks, we investigate the cause of the variations of the galaxy counts in cells. For small cells or cells with a low mean galaxy count, the variation reflects effects from fluctuations in both the matter environment and the halo occupation distribution, while for large cells or cells with a high mean galaxy count, the environment effect dominates. We discuss the implications of our work for investigating galaxy assembly bias.

abstracts.value: One aspect of complexity for quantum many-body systems resides in their ability to exhibit entanglement, uniquely quantum correlations central to quantum computation. To quantitatively explore the diminishing effect that quantum noise has on entanglement resources, we focus on the negativity witness, an entanglement measure based on local time reversal transformations that provides a perfect witness in simple physical contexts. Beyond calculation of the negativity, we analyze the associated eigenvalue spectra of partially transposed density matrices for qudit-qudit bipartitions, finding that higher negativity rank provides greater(reduced) robustness to targeted(depolarizing) noise. In particular, we extend the maximum number of separable states that can be arbitrarily mixed into an entangled pure ensemble while retaining negativity to be exactly equal to the original negativity rank. Furthermore, we report how understanding the role of the negativity rank with respect to the completely depolarizing channel allows direct calculation of (1) certain noise boundaries for the Absolutely Positive Partial Transpose (APPT) subspace beyond which no unitary operator is capable of generating negativity and (2) the maximum qutrit-qutrit APPT purity. Beyond proving tight bounds and contributing to the ongoing search for APPT entanglement, these results expand our understanding of the nuanced relationship between computation with entanglement and practical environments for operating quantum devices.

titles.title: Susceptibility of qudit-qudit entanglement to quantum noise: insights from the negativity rank

abstracts.value: We study the stellar, black hole, and satellite galaxy populations of group- and cluster-scale halos in the IllustrisTNG, TNG-Cluster, and FLAMINGO cosmological hydrodynamical simulations. While normalization differences of up to a factor of two emerge among simulations, many properties exhibit remarkably similar mass-localized slopes, intrinsic scatters, and MPQs across halo samples and redshifts. Correlations among stellar, satellite, and gas properties are generally consistent in sign and their dependence on halo mass and redshift, whereas those involving $M_{\rm BH}$ and $N_{\rm sat}$ show greater variation, particularly in TNG-Cluster. Conditional likelihoods are nearly lognormal for many properties, including $M_{\star,\,\rm tot}$, $N_{\rm sat}$, and $σ_{\rm sat,\,1D}$, while $M_{\star,\,\rm BCG}$ and $M_{\star,\,\rm ICL}$ are negatively skewed. Among the properties considered here, total stellar mass is the best mass proxy, with a halo mass scatter of $7$-$14\%$, followed by $N_{\rm sat}$ with a mass scatter of $9$-$18\%$. Finally, $σ_{\rm sat,\,1D}$ exhibits highly consistent scaling, with mass-independent slope and scatter and a largely neutral correlation structure, suggesting that it is relatively insensitive to astrophysical complexity.

abstracts.value: Femtoscopic correlations in proton-proton and heavy ion collisions are commonly calculated using emission sources from microscopic transport models, where emitted particles are represented by classical phase-space points with simultaneously specified positions and momenta. This point-emitter picture neglects the finite phase-space localization required by quantum mechanics, which can become relevant when the localization scale approaches the femtoscopic source size, particularly in small collision systems. We formulate a quantum treatment by replacing each transport phase-space point with a minimum-uncertainty Gaussian phase-space distribution. Finite localization then induces both spatial and momentum smearing; in the presence of coordinate-momentum correlations, the latter produces a nontrivial modification of the emission source. Using proton--proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=7~\mathrm{TeV}$ simulated with the microscopic Parton--Hadron--String Dynamics transport approach, we show that this effect significantly modifies the proton-pair source and its momentum correlation. Our results expose a quantum localization effect overlooked in transport-based femtoscopy and establish the regime in which the classical point-emitter approximation is valid.

titles.title: Quantum Localization Limit of Transport-Based Femtoscopy

abstracts.value: Spontaneous collapse models provide a possible, testable solution to the quantum measurement problem, but constructing a relativistic version applicable to quantum field theory remains an important open challenge. Challenges in constructing relativistic collapse models include avoiding superluminal signaling and foliation dependence, controlling energy production, and ensuring vacuum stability. Here, we present a relativistic collapse framework that addresses these problems at the cost of introducing a new space of physical states, whose complete characterization is left open. A modified, history-dependent Aharonov--Albert prescription describes instantaneous nonlocal state updates on arbitrary spacelike foliations while preserving foliation independence. To ensure vacuum stability, we modify the standard unitary evolution through a prescription that we name dynamical vacuum subtraction. The resulting dynamical map is linear and trace-preserving but not positive on the full set of standard density operators. We establish no-signaling by proving microscopic parameter independence, and identify conditions under which standard nonrelativistic collapse dynamics are recovered. Finally, we apply our framework to a free massive scalar field, obtaining finite particle-number and energy-increase rates at leading order in the long-time regime, together with further promising evidence for the consistency of the framework.

abstracts.value: We consider the SM extended by a 4th generation of vector-like leptons. This model generates strongly correlated contributions to the lepton masses, Higgs couplings and dipole moments. At leading order the Higgs coupling restricts the magnetic and electric dipole moments to an ellipse. Here we compute the one-loop corrections to the Higgs coupling and two-loop corrections to the dipole moments to obtain the correlation at next-to-leading order using the framework of SMEFT. In addition we resum the leading logarithmic corrections from SM couplings through the SMEFT renormalisation group equations. With these results we compute the RG improved correlation at NLO and discuss the implications for the muon, electron and tau correlations. Specifically, for the muon we find that the corrections contract the ellipse such that a larger part of parameter space becomes compatible with the updated SM value of the muon magnetic moment.

abstracts.value: Effective models make complex quantum dynamics tractable by retaining only the states, processes, and timescales relevant to a given physical question. Their predictive power, however, depends on treating the retained manifold, initial state, observables, micromotion, dissipative channels, and eliminated degrees of freedom consistently. We develop a unified framework for constructing and validating effective descriptions using projection methods, Schrieffer--Wolff transformations, Magnus expansions, adiabatic elimination, small rotations, time coarse graining, and Floquet theory. The quantum Rabi model and its dispersive limits serve as recurring benchmarks for identifying control parameters, virtual processes, spectral corrections, observable dressing, and breakdown. Higher-order resonances and applications to collective light--matter coupling, Raman processes, spin-chain buses, lossy mediators, and driven lattices illustrate how effective interactions can be interpreted and designed. A physical prediction is organized into three order-consistent steps: encoding into the retained description, evolution under the effective dynamics, and reconstruction of the physical observable. This viewpoint exposes failures caused by leakage, small denominators, neglected micromotion, inconsistent observables, memory effects, or incorrectly transformed dissipation, while linking derivation, physical interpretation, and mechanism-guided discovery. Companion notebooks provide QuTiP implementations, convergence tests, and microscopic-to-effective comparisons.

titles.title: Engineering Quantum Interactions: From Effective Models to Validated Physical Predictions

abstracts.value: We study the observational features of thin-disk accretion and emission spectra for static, spherically symmetric dyonic black holes in non-linear electrodynamics (NLED). We also study the kinematic characteristics of particles on circular orbits, such as their angular velocity, specific energy, and specific angular momentum. It is found that modifications of NLED lead to a shrinkage of the ISCO radius, resulting in a shift of the radiation spectrum thermal maximum towards smaller radii and, consequently, an increase in the local effective temperature in comparison with the standard Schwarzschild and Reissner-Nordström solutions. abstracts.value: Polaritons and quantum vacuum dressing are usually regarded as intertwined consequences of ultrastrong light-matter coupling. Here we show that they can be controlled independently through helicity. We consider cyclotron resonance coupled to a chiral cavity supporting a single circular mode. When the helicity of the cavity field matches the cyclotron motion, energy is exchanged resonantly between light and matter, producing a large Rabi splitting and conventional polaritons, while the ground state remains the bare vacuum. Reversing the magnetic field reverses the cyclotron motion without changing the cavity. The same mode then couples through anomalous processes that create and annihilate light and matter excitations in pairs: the conventional polaritonic anticrossing disappears, while the ground state acquires squeezing and virtual excitations. These two regimes show that spectral hybridization and quantum vacuum dressing are distinct manifestations of ultrastrong coupling, and that a large Rabi splitting alone does not imply a dressed quantum vacuum. Helicity therefore provides a route to controlling polariton formation and quantum correlations as distinct resources in cavity quantum materials.

abstracts.value: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) modes have emerged as an important platform for high-dimensional quantum communication but remain vulnerable to environmental noise and channel imperfections. Here we introduce a logical-qubit representation of OAM propagation in which modes evolve as qubits through noisy quantum channels. In this representation, turbulence manifests as leakage from the logical OAM subspace into turbulence-induced leakage components, providing a unified description of degradation in both single-photon and coherent-beam regimes. We show that turbulence-induced leakage exhibits systematic dependence on turbulence strength and OAM order, revealing structured signatures of information redistribution beyond the logical subspace. Leveraging this insight, we develop a distributed quantum feature-extraction scheme that encodes high-dimensional OAM states into quantum representations and employs quantum convolutional operations to extract turbulence-robust features. Simulations and experimental measurements demonstrate robust extraction of these features across a broad range of turbulence strengths, OAM orders, and propagation conditions. Our results establish a direct link between OAM-channel dynamics, structured leakage, and quantum learning, providing a physics-informed framework for characterizing turbulence-degraded high-dimensional optical states and extracting robust signatures of turbulence-induced information redistribution.

titles.title: Structured leakage in OAM-encoded qubits revealed by distributed quantum feature extraction

abstracts.value: The Short-Baseline Near Detector (SBND) is a 112 tonne active mass liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC) situated in the Booster Neutrino Beam at Fermilab, forming part of the Short-Baseline Neutrino (SBN) Program. SBND began operation in 2024 and has since accumulated the world's largest sample of neutrino-argon interactions. This paper describes the as-built detector and presents performance results from the first year of beam operation. All detector systems performed at or above design requirements. The liquid argon purity achieved an electron lifetime exceeding 30ms, ten times the design requirement, for more than 95% of Run 1. The TPC wire plane readout achieved noise levels at the theoretical minimum for the given wire geometry (an average of 388e$^-$ for the 4m long collection plane wires) with 99.3% of readout channels live. Together, the liquid argon purity and TPC performance are enabling extremely clean event reconstruction in the SBND TPC. The photon detection system, consisting of passive reflectors and multiple active components (PMTs and X-ARAPUCAs), has achieved a light yield exceeding 10 photoelectrons per MeV throughout the detector volume and a timing resolution of a few nanoseconds, sufficient to resolve the 19ns bunch structure of the Booster Neutrino Beam. A nearly 4$π$ cosmic ray tagger system surrounds the TPC to mitigate cosmic backgrounds in neutrino and BSM physics analyses. The data acquisition system has demonstrated stable performance up to an event rate of 8Hz, and a data collection efficiency of 98.6% was achieved throughout SBND's first neutrino run in 2025. These results demonstrate that SBND represents the state of the art in multi-tonne-scale LArTPC detector performance.

titles.title: Short-Baseline Near Detector (SBND): Design and Initial Performance

abstracts.value: The possible antimagnetic rotation in the <math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>46</mn></mrow></math> odd-<math><mi>A</mi></math> isotones <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Rb</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>83</mn></mmultiscripts></math> and <math><mmultiscripts><mi mathvariant="normal">Y</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>85</mn></mmultiscripts></math> is investigated using the cranked shell model combined with a particle-number-conserving method. For the positive-parity yrast bands in the two isotones, the angular-momentum alignments are reproduced well. The configurations of high-spin part in both bands are determined as <math><mrow><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>⊗</mo><mi>ν</mi><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, by analyzing the occupation probability of each cranked Nilsson orbital near the Fermi surface. The calculated <math><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>E</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> values are small and decrease with the increasing rotational frequency, in agreement with the experiments; meanwhile, the two-shears-like mechanism is exhibited clearly. Therefore, the high-spin parts of the two bands, built on <math><mrow><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>⊗</mo><mi>ν</mi><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> configuration, match the criteria of antimagnetic rotation, which is the first time that the antimagnetic rotation is revealed for odd-<math><mi>A</mi></math> nuclei in the <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow></math> mass region.

abstracts.value: Constructing optimal entanglement witnesses for arbitrary quantum systems remains a formidable challenge, hindered by the structural complexity of high-dimensional quantum state spaces. In this work we overcome this barrier by introducing a unified framework for constructing geometrically optimal witnesses capable of identifying arbitrary entanglement structures. By leveraging the geometric properties of a target quantum state relative to a specific entanglement structure in Hilbert-Schmidt space, these witnesses are constructed in an efficient and effective manner. Among all nontrivial witnesses, they provide maximal distinguishability between the target state and the set of states without the desired entanglement structure. As a result, our approach enables the universal detection of bipartite, multipartite, and high-dimensional entanglement. To demonstrate its experimental feasibility, we apply the framework to a four-qubit nuclear spin quantum system. Compared to existing methods, our approach offers enhanced noise robustness, broader detection universality, and improved construction efficiency, providing a powerful and versatile tool for advancing the characterization and understanding of entanglement in quantum systems.

titles.title: Universal entanglement detection with geometrically optimal witnesses

abstracts.value: Qudits can be described by a state vector in a q-dimensional Hilbert space, enabling a more extensive encoding and manipulation of information compared to qubits. This implies that conducting fault-tolerant quantum computations using qudits rather than qubits might entail less overhead. In this work, I investigate the viability of qudits across three key components of a fault-tolerant quantum computer: hardware control, quantum error-correction codes, and logical gate operations. This includes benchmarking physically decomposed qudit gates against qubit-based implementations for a specific donor-spin system, threshold simulations of qudit error-correction codes using tailored simulators and decoders, and simulations of magic state distillation circuits with qudits.At the hardware level, a numerical leakage-aware randomized benchmarking protocol is applied to a native ququart encoding in a donor-spin system and compared against an equivalent pair of encoded qubits. The ququart implementation is found to reduce the lower-bound gate infidelity by 40 – 50%, a consequence of the fewer ESR and EDSR pulses and correspondingly lower cumulative noise exposure. This provides a concrete, platform-specific demonstration of reduced physical-gate overhead prior to the introduction of any error-correction redundancy.At the level of quantum error correction, the viability of qudits is investigated through the construction and simulation of the quantum circuits for the five-qudit perfect code. The code is evaluated under a multidimensional circuit-level noise model using decoders specifically adapted to the qudit setting. This yields the first threshold estimates reported for qutrit and ququint codes under circuit-level noise. After introducing a flag qudit to protect the code from hook errors, comparable error thresholds of the order of 10–4 are obtained for qudits of dimensions 2, 3 and 5. These simulations were subsequently performed using Sdim, a stabilizer tableau simulator that enabled threshold estimation up to dimension q = 7, a regime inaccessible to state-vector simulators such as Cirq.At the level of logical operations, magic state distillation protocols of the Bravyi-Kitaev type are simulated under logical circuit-level noise, to my knowledge for the first time for this protocol family. Once the Clifford operations implementing the distillation circuit are subject to a nonzero logical error rate, the achievable output fidelity saturates within a finite usable distillation range rather than an arbitrarily improvable one: roughly 0.9-15.6% for the |T⟩₂-type protocol, 3.7-5% for the |H⟩₂-type protocol and 5.4-7.4% for the |H+⟩₃-type protocol at a representative logical circuit-level noise level of pCL = 10–3. The qutrit protocol achieves a more favorable distillation threshold but suffers from a substantially lower yield due to its reduced syndrome acceptance probability. This highlights a trade-off between threshold performance and yield that is intrinsic to the higher-dimensional construction. Further investigation with more advanced and larger-scale protocols is required to better understand and characterize this behavior.Overall, these results show that qudits can provide real efficiency benefits: higher-dimensional control can improve physical gate fidelity, and qutrit and ququint error-correction thresholds can match those of qubits when hook errors are properly handled. However, logical circuit-level noise limits the maximum magic state fidelity, showing that the benefits of qudits are not yet fully realized at the logical-operation level. This thesis provides the first broad numerical study of these effects and introduces the simulation tools needed to explore larger code families, decoders, and distillation protocols.

titles.title: Using qudits for fault-tolerant quantum computing

Abstract

The neutron lifetime is an essential parameter in Big Bang nucleosynthesis. It also helps
to determine the element Vud of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix in the
Standard Model of particle physics that represents the up and down quark coupling that
occurs through the weak force. Currently, a 4σ discrepancy exists between beam and trap
lifetime experiments. The Precision Experiment on the Neutron Lifetime Operating with
Proton Extraction (PENeLOPE) is a magneto-gravitational ultracold neutron (UCN) trap
experiment that aims to measure the neutron lifetime with a precision of 0.1 s. Two butterfly
shutters were tested as UCN source and storage valves in PENeLOPEs configuration. Their
average relative leak rates—corrected for background and normalized to the UCN source
transmission rate—were 2.23±1.10 % and 1.01±0.85 %, demonstrating their inadequacy for
the intended purpose. PENeLOPE has stainless steel storage surfaces which can depolarize
UCNs on wall bounce. This affects the systematic uncertainty on the neutron lifetime mea-
surement. Simulations showed the precision goal would be met with a stainless-steel UCN
spin-flip probability (βSS) of 10−5, resulting in a 0.0442 ± 0.0019 s systematic shift of the
neutron lifetime created by marginally trapped UCNs. Fourteen PENeLOPE experiment
runs yielded a statistical precision of 0.0964 ± 0.0012 s, with PENeLOPE installed at the
planned UCN source at Research Neutron Source Heinz Maier-Leibnitz (FRM II) located in
Munich, Germany [1]. Higher βSS values caused prohibitively large systematic shifts, which
could be mitigated by nickel-phosphorous coating to reduce the UCN spin-flip probability
of PENeLOPE’s storage surfaces.

Keywords: Ultracold Neutrons; PENeLOPE; neutron lifetime; UCN

1.1.2 Big Bang Nucleosynthesis

In cosmology, the neutron lifetime influences the abundance ratios of primordial light ele-
ments. Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) is the era when primordial light elements began
to form. At the onset of BBN, the Universe consisted of a hot dense soup of particles inter-
acting with one another in equilibrium. As the Universe expanded, it began to cool down,
corresponding to particles decreasing in kinetic energy energy throughout the Universe from
initially deciseconds to around 200 seconds after the singularity.

Over the last few decades, two methods have been used to determine the lifetime of the free
neutron: beam and trap experiments.

Beam experiments measure the number of neutrons in a specific volume from a neutron flux
and detect the decay particles per second in that volume. The rate of neutron decay Ṅ can

1.2.1 Strong Force

Fermi was the first to propose that UCNs could completely reflect off material surfaces at any
incident angle [19]. This phenomenon arises from the scattering interaction of an incident
neutron with a collection of nuclei, mediated by the strong nuclear force. The probability
of reflection is determined from the neutron’s wave function. Since the exact potential for
a collection of nuclei is computationally complex and impractical to determine, an effective
potential is employed in the calculation to approximate the neutron wave function. By
using this simplified potential, the Schrödinger equation becomes solvable to obtain an
approximate wavefunction; however, its validity is restricted to low-energy regimes and
regions far from the interaction point [20]. Near the interaction region, the wave function
serves only as an approximation, but it is sufficiently accurate to reproduce key scattering
observables, such as cross-sections.

The theoretical predictions for scattering observables, such as cross-sections and re-
flection probabilities, can be directly compared to experimental results. If the predictions

Spin-flips due to Wall Reflections

When a neutron interacts with a material wall, two types of spin-dependent scattering can
occur: coherent and incoherent scattering. Coherent scattering arises from constructive in-
terference of scattering amplitudes from all nuclei and depends on the average scattering
length, independent of nuclear spin I, reflecting the material’s collective structure. In con-
trast, incoherent scattering stems from variations in individual scattering lengths due to
nuclear spin states or isotopic differences, explicitly depending on the relative spin orien-
tations of the neutron spin Sn and nucleus I. Spin-flip transitions in incoherent scattering
occur through quantum mechanical spin coupling, where three out of four possible spin
configurations of aligned or anti-aligned nuclear spin and neutron spin involve spin flips
(anti-aligned states are related to spin flips), leading to a dominant 2

3 contribution of spin-
flip cross-section to the total incoherent scattering cross-section [24].

15



For characterizing depolarization probability from neutron and material surface interac-
tions, each unique material surface has an associated spin-flip probability per wall bounce
β that is found experimentally. For materials used in UCN experiments, β is typically in
the order of ∼ 10−6 [24, 25]. Experiments that characterize β for different materials can
vary in the strength of the magnetic field used for holding the spin from mT to T ranges of
magnetic field strength.

1.2.4 Weak Force

The weak force is responsible for β-decay as mentioned earlier in Section 1.1. The other forces
that act on UCNs are able to confine or contain them while the weak force is responsible for
their decay process. UCNs with their extremely low kinetic energies, are ideal for precision
studies of the weak interaction due to their ability to be confined in material, magnetic, or
gravitational traps for extended periods.

PENeLOPE

2.1 Magneto-gravitational trap

The Precision Experiment on the Neutron Lifetime Operating with Proton Extraction (PENe-
LOPE) is a magneto-gravitational trap experiment. PENeLOPE’s objective is to measure
τn with a precision of 0.1 s. The configuration of the experiment is shown in Figure 2.1.
The magnetic field used to store neutrons is created by twenty-four alternating solenoid
coils housing a cylindrical shell storage volume. The coils are made from NbTi wires with
between 32-58 winding layers. The coils are cooled down by a liquid helium cryostat below
the superconducting transition temperature of Tc ∼10 K. The cryostat helium reservoir,
coils and storage volume are protected by a radiation shield surrounding the cylindrical
volume, which is also encased in a vacuum vessel. The inner vertically stacked coils have an
outer radius of around 146 mm and the outer vertically stacked coils have an inner radius
of a little over 500 mm.

17



Figure 2.1: Rendering of the PENeLOPE experiment. Figure reproduced from Schreyer [2].

There are 11 outer, 9 inner, and 4 bottom cylindrical coils that function to create large
magnetic field gradients at the edge of the UCN storage volume. The nominal current
through the coils produces a magnetic field strength of up to 5.5 T, but the usable field
is only 1.8 T due to large gradients within the storage volume. Figure 2.2 is a vertical cut
through PENeLOPE’s storage volume, with the coils represented by blue rectangles within
the storage walls. The field lines produced by the coils are seen as black lines around the
coils. The strength of the magnetic field inside of the storage volume is highest near the
coils and decreases towards the center of the storage volume. Low-Field Seekers (LFSs)

18



may be magnetically trapped within this low field region to eliminate or reduce their losses
resulting from interactions with material surfaces. Conversely, High-Field Seekers (HFSs)
will have a high chance of loss as they are attracted to the high field strength regions near
the coils, where they will repeatedly interact with the material walls. The zero field regions,
colored red on the left side of Fig. 2.2, do not maintain the adiabatic condition, Eq. 1.21,
allowing UCNs to spin-flip. UCN spin-flipping within the trapping region must be avoided
as it affects the UCN population significantly. A large central current of at least 12.5 kA
running up the center of the experiment is introduced, producing an azimuthal spin-holding
magnetic field covering these zero-field regions.

LFSs are trapped by a combination of electromagnetic and gravitational interactions
with minimal to no contact with the material surfaces during storage. The
magneto-gravitational trapping potential is

Vtrap = ±µnB + mngh , (2.1)

where the positive magnetic potential is relevant for trapping the LFS population in the

of Fig. 2.2, the trajectory of an LFS with energy near the maximum trappable potential is

2.2 Polarizer & Spin-Flipper

2.2.1 Polarizer

PENeLOPE’s ability to only trap the LFS without wall interactions favors filling polarized
neutrons into its storage volume. The polarization

be large enough so that the losses from HFSs do not reduce the measured storage lifetime
of all neutrons significantly [2]. This can be achieved by adding a HFS cleaning period to
PENeLOPE before the measurement starts (see Section 2.6) and improved by pre-polarizing
the neutrons upon filling. This is shown in Fig. 2.1 as a polarizer installed in the UCN source
guide.

The polarizer that is most cost-effective is a ferromagnetic film. An external magnetic
field produced by permanent or electromagnets can saturate the magnetic field in an Al foil
coated with an iron film. The UCN traversing the foil will see a potential of

V± = VF ± µnBS , (2.3)

20



where Bs is the saturated magnetic field, VF is the Fermi potential of the film typically Iron
with a Fermi potential value of VF = 209 neV. The saturated field produced in an iron film
is 2.16 T which creates a magnetic potential of 130 neV [2]. LFSs will encounter a potential
barrier of V+ = 340 neV, which they cannot overcome since doing so would require kinetic
energies exceeding the UCN energy region. The HFS population will see V− = 89 neV, and
if they have kinetic energies above 89 neV they will be able to pass through the film. This
provides the HFS population with a high transmission through the film for higher efficiency.

2.2.2 Spin-Flipper

The thin-film polarizer would allow the undesirable HFSs into PENeLOPE’s storage volume
so their spins must be reversed by a spin flipper. The method for spin-flipping used is the
adiabatic fast-passage (AFP): it allows spin reversal of low velocity UCN inside a gradient
magnetic field. The AFP consists of two magnetic fields. One magnetic field Bo holds the
spin in the ẑ direction in which the neutron spin precesses around while a perpendicular
magnetic field, B1 rotates around Bo with frequency ω. To follow spin orientation over time,
the Bloch equation,

be decomposed into two counter-rotating fields where one is in the same direction as the
particle’s spin precession driving the spin flip and the other rotating field is in the opposite
direction of the particle’s spin precession and does not contribute to spin flips.

2.3 Absorber rings

UCNs from the source entering PENeLOPE’s storage volume may have energies above
the magnetic trapping potential. The UCNs that have energies above this potential, but
also have energies below the Fermi potential of the material surfaces, are called marginally
trapped (MT) neutrons because they are not completely contained by the magnetic field
and are able to interact with the storage walls. MT UCNs then have a loss probability per
wall bounce which could reduce the measured storage lifetime measurement τ < τn. In order

21



to minimize the systematic effects that arise from MT UCNs, an absorber is added within
the storage volume in order to reduce the UCN population with total energies higher than
the 115 neV trapping potential. The absorbers will be either titanium which is a neutron
absorber or polyethylene which upscatters neutrons. Both materials have imaginary Fermi
potentials close to or smaller than zero (VTi = −51 neV, VPE = −8.7 neV).

The absorbers shall be in place during the material storage stage of PENeLOPE, when
the main storage magnet is turned off. During the magnetic storage stage, the absorbers
shall be hidden behind the magnetic field for all magnetically trapped neutrons. This only
leaves small spaces of high magnetic field strength close to the storage volume walls. They
are concentric cylindrical shells or rings with a thickness of a few millimeters and are
positioned near the inner and outer surfaces of the storage volume as seen in Fig. 2.1. The
lower edge of the absorbers is situated at a height of about 700 mm from the bottom of the
storage volume to cut off the UCN energy spectrum to ∼80 neV (for the nominal current
of 283.5 A) after filling the storage volume.

During an experiment cycle, the magnetic field will be turned on and off creating a shift
of energy from heating and cooling the polarized UCNs and a cut-off of 80 neV prevents
the heating of UCN above 115 neV. After ramping up the magnetic field, the HFSs that are
constrained to propagate along the material walls undergo many reflections which increases
the probability of spin flips during wall interaction. Since the magnetic field at the walls is
quite large, the HFS might gain a lot of kinetic energy when the spin flips, turning them
into marginally trapped LFS UCN. This can lead to a higher measured storage lifetime.
A side view of HFSs and magnetically trapped LFSs inside PENeLOPE’s storage volume
when the magnetic field is turned on is shown in Figure 2.3. To reduce the HFS population,
the absorber rings will move vertically down along the wall to a position close to the bottom
of the storage volume of ∼5 mm as more HFSs can reach this location. To allow this vertical
movement, actuators will be installed on top of the storage volume attaching to the rings.

2.5 The UCN Source at FRM II

Before moving to TRIUMF in Summer 2024, PENeLOPE was anticipated to be installed
at the Forschungs-Neutronenquelle Heinz Maier-Leibnitz (FRM II) UCN source located
at the Technical University of Munich (TUM). The source operates on the principle of
superthermal UCN production and utilizes a solid deuterium (sD2) converter as its core
technology.

24



Figure 2.5: Schematic representation of the FRM II UCN source. The solid deuterium (sD2)

The UCN source is integrated into the SR6 beamline at FRM II [1]. At its heart is a
toroidal, double-walled aluminum converter vessel, which is maintained at a temperature of
5 K using a supercritical helium cooling loop. To enhance the efficiency of neutron conver-
sion, solid hydrogen (sH2) is used as a premoderator, cooling incoming thermal neutrons
to approximately 40 K before they interact with the sD2 converter. Solid deuterium, frozen
onto the vessels walls by resublimation, facilitates the conversion of thermal neutrons into
UCNs through phonon excitation processes in the crystal lattice.

Thermal neutrons from the reactor, upon entering the sD2 lattice, lose their kinetic en-
ergy through solid-state excitations and are converted into ultracold neutrons with energies
below 230 neV. The produced UCNs are then extracted from the converter and transported
via beamline guides to the experiments. These guides are designed to minimize UCN losses,
with transport efficiencies of 99% per meter for neutrons in the energy range of 100–200 neV.

The source is currently in the non-nuclear testing stage before installing and commis-
sioning at FRM II. It is expected to deliver a flux density of 6×105 UCN/cm2/s at the SR6

25



A-side beam port. This flux density is used for simulations of PENeLOPE installed at the
FRM II UCN source in Chapter 4.

2.6 PENeLOPE Experiment Cycle

PENeLOPE’s foreseen experiment cycle is similar to all bottle experiments with the trap
method, which includes filling, storing, and counting. However, more stages are included:
two ramping stages for turning the magnetic field on or off, and two stages for cleaning out
unwanted UCN from the storage volume. PENeLOPE’s experiment cycle consists of seven
stages in total. Approximate stage durations are given in brackets.

1. Filling (∼200 s): UCNs are transported from a source to PENeLOPE’s storage volume.

2. Marginally-trapped (MT) cleaning (∼200 s): The storage valve is closed. UCNs in the
storage volume with energies above the magnetic trapping potential are removed by
absorber rings placed at a certain height within the trap.

3. Ramp-up (100 s): The coil current is increased to the nominal current which produces
the magnetic trapping potential.

4. High-field Seeker Cleaning (∼60 s): HFSs populate the region close to the storage
walls. They are cleaned out through an absorber moving from top to bottom near the
inner and outer surfaces of the storage volume.

5. Storage (∼20-1550 s): UCNs are stored within the storage volume for two predefined
durations (t1 and t2) to calculate τ with a short and long storage time. The proton
detector counts the decay protons that are produced only during this stage.

6. Ramp-down (100 s): The magnetic field is turned off over a span of 100 s for trapped
UCN to exit the storage volume for counting.

7. Counting (∼300 s): UCN are given time to reach the detector after exiting the storage
volume.

Certain components are moved or turned on during different stages such as the UCN
Switch flap. Table 2.1 shows the component configuration in each stage. The UCN switch
flap has three positions: The filling position allows UCN to propagate to the storage volume
closing off their path to the UCN detector, the middle position opens the path from both
the UCN source volume and to the UCN detector, and the detector position allows UCN to
propagate from the storage volume to the UCN detector blocking off the path to the UCN
source. The next subsections contain a detailed description of all cycles.

2.6.1 Filling

The filling stage is the first stage in the experiment cycle during which UCNs are transported
from the anticipated UCN source at the FRM II into PENeLOPE’s storage volume. The
energy spectrum of the source plays a significant role, since PENeLOPE should be placed
at a height, where the maximum of the spectrum can be magnetically stored inside the
experiment, balanced by gravity. Guides that have VF > En are used to propagate UCNs
into the storage volume. The source and storage valves are open and the UCN switch directs
UCNs from the source to the storage volume. The UCNs are polarized after entering the
guide from the source before reaching the switch. A spin holding field, created by a current
flowing through the central rod, maintains UCN polarization once they enter into the storage
volume. The magnetic field created by the superconducting magnet to store UCNs is not on
at this time, so UCNs in the storage volume will interact with the inner and outer surface
walls of the storage volume.

2.6.2 Marginally Trapped UCN Cleaning

After the filling stage, the storage valve is closed and marginally trapped UCNs—those
with total energies exceeding the equipotential limit of ∼115 neV (only at nominal current)
imposed by the magneto-gravitational field—are removed. The UCN switch flap is then ro-
tated into the middle position to dump the remaining UCNs in the guides into the detector.
The absorber rings, placed at 700 mm above the bottom of the storage volume, remove
these UCNs leaving the UCNs in the storage volume with maximum total energies under
∼80 neV. The reason for setting the absorbers at that specific height will be explained in
section 2.6.3. The absorbers’ positions may be changed to cut off the energy spectrum at
other energies if needed. In the current configuration, the absorber is kept at a height of
∼700 mm above the bottom of the storage volume from the start of filling and continuing
until a certain cleaning time to sufficiently clean the MT UCN population.

27



2.6.3 Magnetic Field Ramp-up

At the beginning of the ramp-up stage, the UCN switch flap remains in its position to
open the path between the storage volume and the UCN detector. Since the storage valve
remains closed, the UCN detected at this point would be any that come from leaks through
the valves or background. A magnetic field is introduced by increasing the current through
the superconducting coils. The magnetic field increases over a span of 100 s until the nominal
current is reached. As the magnetic field strength increases, the total energy of UCNs is
altered due to the time-varying magnetic potential. This potential acts as a dynamic barrier,
effectively behaving as a moving mirror in the reference frame of the UCNs. Depending on
the phase of interaction, UCNs reflecting off this moving potential experience a change in
momentum, leading to either a gain or loss of kinetic energy. LFSs are heated or gain total
energy while the HFSs are cooled or lose total energy. By the end of this stage the LFSs
with total energies under 115 neV are completely trapped within the equipotential lines as
shown on the left side of Fig. 2.2. LFSs with higher total energies that are not completely
trapped within the equipotential lines are considered MT UCNs that still interact with
the material walls. The HFS population is attracted to regions close to the material walls
subjecting the HFS population to have more losses than the LFS population through wall
interactions.

2.6.4 High-field Seeker Cleaning

Once the magnetic field reaches its maximum value, the HFSs are removed via absorbers.
They are not trapped by the magneto-gravitational field within the storage volume at any
total energy. The absorber rings remove the HFSs by lowering down from their height of
∼700 mm to ∼5 mm above the bottom of the storage volume and are held there for roughly
20 s until they are brought back up to 700 mm. The storage valve is opened at the start of
this stage to release any marginally trapped UCNs or HFSs into the detector, serving both
to remove these unwanted UCNs and to provide a comparative measurement between runs.
The fully trapped LFSs are contained by the magnetic field and gravity so they should only
experience losses through β−decay during this stage even with the absorbers moving up
and down as long as it does not cross the 115 neV equipotential line. The proton detector
is activated during this stage to provide insight on how the population changes.

2.6.5 Storage

The storage stage starts after the HFS cleaning stage with a majority of fully trapped LFSs
plus a smaller fraction of the partially trapped MT UCNs and/or HFSs within the storage
volume. The absorbers stay at 700 mm, the magnetic field is held constant, the storage valve
stays open, and the UCN switch connects the storage volume to the UCN detector. The
proton detector is operational during the entirety of this stage to detect the decay protons

28



from UCN β−decay. For a full experiment cycle, the storage durations are t1 = 20 s and
t2 = 1550 s for this study, similar to the UCNτ experiment [13]. Systematic effects arise
from losses of marginally trapped UCNs and high-field seekers within the storage volume
during this stage.

2.6.6 Magnetic Field Ramp-down

After storage the remaining surviving UCN need to be counted in the UCN detector which
requires the magnetic field to be turned off. The UCN switch, storage valve, and absorber
remain in the same position as during the storage stage. The magnetic field is then decreased
slowly over 100 s until completely off. The detection of UCN starts during this stage. As the
magneto-gravitational equipotential barrier decreases, all UCNs, including those previously
trapped magnetically, are able to exit the storage volume and are guided to the UCN
detector.

2.6.7 Counting

Once the magnetic field is turned off, the remaining UCN within the storage volume are
given time to reach the detector. During this stage, the UCN switch, storage valve, and
absorber are in the same configuration as the previous stage. At this point, no distinction
between HFSs and LFSs is made since the detection is not spin sensitive. The final UCN
count is then acquired from the portion of UCN that were able to be detected. N1 and N2

from Eq. 1.10 are determined from the background corrected integral of UCN counts during
the ramp-down and counting stage for t1 and t2, respectively. The losses of UCN along the
way to the detector is modeled by a collection efficiency through simulations.

Characterization

Three components at Technische Universität München (TUM) were available as viable can-
didates for PENeLOPE’s neutron transport between a UCN source, trap volume, and UCN
detector: a replica UCN guide, and two butterfly shutters. It was necessary to characterize
them to see if they were suitable for PENeLOPE’s τn measurement goal. We measured
the storage lifetime in the replica guide and the leak rates of the butterfly shutters. These
experiments were conducted at the TRIGA (Training Research Isotope production Gen-
eral Atomics) reactor in Mainz, Germany on September 2022. The TRIGA reactor will be
discussed in Section 3.2.1.

3.1 UCN Transport Components

UCN storage experiment cycles typically start with neutrons being transported from a
source to a storage volume. UCN transport components must be enclosed, such as cylindrical
guides with surface Fermi potential values large enough to allow UCNs to propagate while
reflecting off their inner surfaces. The enclosed volume must also have a suitable vacuum for
neutrons to have a low enough probability of being absorbed by rest gas. The reflectivity
of the guides plays a crucial role in the UCN transport efficiency, with surface roughness
being a key factor. Rough surfaces result in non-specular reflections, where neutrons scatter
in random directions rather than reflecting uniformly, causing a diffusive transport process.
This increases the number of reflections required for a neutron to travel a specific distance,
unlike smooth surfaces that enable specular reflection, thereby significantly reducing the
transmission efficiency of the guide. To address these challenges, extensive research and
development efforts are underway at various laboratories to enhance the properties of UCN
guides [26].

One method to achieve a guide with a smooth surface and high Fermi potential involves
replicating the glass-like smoothness onto nickel composites to fabricate replica guides. By

3.1.1 Replica Guide

Replica guides, as shown in Fig. 3.1, have been shown to have good UCN transport charac-

Sputter-Dünnschichttechnik Heidelberg (SD-H). They are made of a nickel-vanadium (NiV)
thin film alloy composition consisting of 93% nickel and 7% vanadium. To produce a replica
guide, a thin film is sputtered onto glass to a thickness of ∼100 nm and then a backing
composition of pure nickel is used to support the film resulting in a combined thickness
of 0.5 mm [27]. The alloy is then peeled off the glass and rolled. The backing is welded
along the rolled alloy’s length to form a cylinder with an inner diameter of 115 mm. This
thin-walled tube is not able to sustain a pressure difference of 1 bar so it is necessary to
enclose it within a stainless steel vacuum enclosure. The guides have a Fermi potential of
∼252 neV. Their surface roughness of under 10 Å[26] is equivalent to the roughness of the
original glass as it was copied from the sputtering. UCNs that propagate through the guide
still have a probability of being absorbed or upscattered with each wall interaction. During
the characterization experiment in Mainz, four 0.5 m replica guides were installed in series
to form a 2 m long storage volume.

3.2 Source Guide Characterization

3.2.1 TRIGA Reactor and UCN Source

The TRIGA reactor at Mainz offers two modes of operation, the first being a steady
state mode or continuous operation at 100 kW that provides a thermal neutron flux of
1012 n/(cm2 s). The other is a pulse mode which increases the instantaneous neutron flux
up to 250 MW within a 30 ms window 12 times per hour. The peak flux of neutrons is
up to 2 × 1015 n/cm2 s. The reactor core fuel elements have a chemical composition of
Uranium(20 % 235U)-Zirconiumhydride(UZrH) [28]. The hydrogen acts as a moderator,
providing inherent safety if the fuel elements increase in temperature. The neutrons pro-
duced during the heating will increase in energy, resulting in lower fission reaction rates until
fission is stopped completely. Figure 3.3 shows a horizontal cross-section of the reactor core
with beamports to guide neutrons out from the core. UCNs are produced at beamports C
and D. Beamport C was used for the PENeLOPE component characterization experiments.

3.2.4 UCN detector

The detector used in these experiments is a cascade UCN detector [31]. The cascade detector
is able to detect a UCN flux on the order of 107n/cm2s. It has an Al foil entrance window
with a Fermi potential of 54 neV and a thickness of 100 µm. Neutrons that pass through
the window interact with a 10B layer coated on a drift electrode leading to the reactions

10B + n −→ 7Li + α + 2.79 MeV (6%), (3.2)

and
10B + n −→ 7Li + α + 2.31 MeV (94%). (3.3)

The products from these reactions then ionize atoms in a gas mixture inside of the reaction
chamber, typically argon and carbon dioxide, ArCO2. The ionized atoms then interact with
gas electron multiplier (GEM) foils creating electrons. These electrons are then amplified
by being accelerating through an electric field in the holes between the GEM foils. The
amplified electrons then drift to a printed circuit board (PCB) readout. The PCB readout
is a key part of the electronic system, designed to capture, amplify, and transmit data about
neutron interactions occurring in the detector.

than uniformly influencing all counts across multiple runs with a single storage time.

the BS1 leak are left within the apparatus reaching all the way to the detector. The last
stage of the experiment is a measurement of transmission counts with all shutters opened

3.2.6 Filling Time Optimization

The optimum filling time was found by measuring the saturation curve shown in Figure 3.13
of neutrons filled into the storage volume and then immediately emptied into the detector.
Neutron counts were recorded for various filling times {0 s, 4 s, 6 s, 8 s, 10 s, 20 s, 30 s,
40 s, 50 s}. Two or three runs were conducted for each of the filling times in an overall
randomized order of 23 runs and were plotted by averaging neutron counts obtained for
each predetermined filling time. The durations of the other stages were held constant for
each run: tstore = 10 s, tcounting = 80 s, and ttransmission = 50 s. tfill = 20 s was chosen as a
compromise between reaching saturation in the number of neutrons stored and saving time
as shorter filling durations allow more cycle runs in the same amount of time.

The BS1 and BS2 shutter leak experiments were conducted separately with the same set
up, once with BS1 and once with BS2. The leak rate measurements were obtained through
the four different configurations shown in Tbl. 3.2: 1. Both shutters were open for a trans-

3.2.9 Storage Lifetime Experiment Analysis & Results

The storage lifetime is determined by filling neutrons into a trap, holding them for varying
storage times tstore and counting the surviving neutrons in a detector. The experiment was
conducted on two different days, designated Day 1 and Day 2.

Other measurements include background (BG) counts and BS1 UCN leak counts. BG
counts may come from different sources such as electronic BG that is always there, a cold
and faster neutron BG that come from when the reactor and UCN source are operational,
and a BG due to leaks through valves which is present when the reactor and UCN source are
operational but suppressed when more than 1 valve is closed. The cold and faster neutron
BG differs from the BG due to leaks through valves because cold neutrons do not have the

44



same property as UCNs of being totally reflected at any incident angle off a surface, so cold
and faster neutrons have a chance to interact with the guide surfaces but are not contained
like UCNs. The best period for background determination is the storage period, where both
shutters BS1 and BS2 were closed as seen in Fig. 3.10. The BG measured during the storage
period takes into consideration all the possible BGs that were mentioned above. These BG
measurements during storage are used to find an overall BG which includes a count from the
UCN leak through BS2 measured as well during the storage stage. The BS1 and BS2 leaks
affect the overall detected population. The BS1 leak during the storage period is illustrated
in Fig. 3.10. UCNs can propagate through a closed BS1 from both directions from the source
to the storage volume or from the storage volume to the source. The effect of UCNs leaving
the storage volume through BS leaks influences the measurement of τst. The incoming UCNs
from the source that leak into the storage volume provide a net positive effect since UCN
density will be higher upstream of BS1 compared to downstream (storage volume), so the
BS1 leak into the storage volume is constant since the source provides a constant flux. This
complicates the τst calculation through having a N(tstore) measurement that includes these
UCN gains and losses during storage.

attributed to several factors: 1) gaps between the 0.5 m sections of the replica guides 2)
gaps in the butterfly valves when closed 3) losses in the bulk of the surfaces of the valves,
adapters and / or replica guides. It is hard to quantify 1 or 3, but a calculation can be made
to estimate 2. If the transmission of the closed valve is around 2 % of the open position, one
could define an effective opening of 2 % of its opening cross section that takes into account
all leak mechanisms such as the transmission through the bulk of the valve material. Taking
the geometry into account, one can then calculate the lifetime due to this effective opening.

Chapter Summary

This chapter focuses on analyzing three critical factors to determine whether the measure-
ment of the neutron lifetime using PENeLOPE can achieve the target precision of 0.1 s.
The following factors are examined:

1. Systematic Effects and Marginally Trapped (MT) UCN: Some UCNs are not
fully trappable within PENeLOPE, leading to systematic shifts in the measured neutron
lifetime. Of particular focus in this work is the contribution of marginally trapped (MT)
UCNs with total energies exceeding the magneto-gravitational trapping potential of 115 neV.
These neutrons may be lost during storage and cause shifts in the neutron lifetime mea-
surement. To address this issue, the duration of the MT cleaning stage, described in Section
2.6, is optimized to reduce the MT UCN population and minimize its impact on the mea-
surement.

2. Spin-Flip Probability of Stainless Steel: The walls of PENeLOPE’s storage volume
are composed of stainless steel, and UCN interactions with the storage walls can cause neu-
tron spin flips. This affects the ratio of low-field seekers to high-field seekers in PENeLOPE.
The spin-flip probability per wall bounce of stainless steel (βSS) is not well known. Only one
published result of βSS = 3.36 × 10−3 can be found and only in a conference presentation
that was not peer reviewed [24, 38]. This value is more than two orders of magnitude higher
than other β values for typical UCN component materials listed in Table 4.2. Due to the
potential uncertainty in this measurement, a parameter sweep of βSS with three values of
2 × 10−3, 10−4 and 10−5 was performed. A higher spin flip probability affects the viability
of PENeLOPE dramatically as will be shown in Section 4.3.3.

3. Number of Cycles Needed to Achieve a Statistical Precsion of 0.1 s: Section
4.3.4 presents the number of experimental cycles necessary to reach a statistical precision of

53



0.1 s on the neutron lifetime assuming PENeLOPE is operated at the planned UCN source
at the FRM II.

Methodology Employed

The method for analyzing the precision of the neutron lifetime measured using PENeLOPE
involves several steps. To start, simulations of UCNs in PENeLOPE are performed using
the PENTrack program, described in the next Section 4.1, to emulate full PENeLOPE
experiment cycles. Each of the seven stages of the experiment cycle, described in Section
2.6, are simulated independently. This is necessary since the stage durations need to be
varied to achieve an optimal compromise between statistical sensitivity and systematic
effects. To this end, the neutron population in PENeLOPE is divided up into 5 neV energy
bins and into low-field seekers (LFSs) and high-field seekers (HFSs). The assumption here
is that UCNs are characterized sufficiently by sorting them into a specific energy and spin
orientation bin. This is valid since the nature of diffuse wall reflections randomized neutron
trajectories efficiently so that the phase space of neutrons is in equilibrium. In practical
terms, this means that any neutron in a particular bin, no matter its location and velocity
vector has an almost equal probability of reaching any other accessible location in the
experiment. To properly connect one experimental stage to the next, a survival probability
is calculated for each energy bin which is used to evolve the energy distribution for LFSs and
HFSs through all seven stages. These distributions are created at each full second during
the whole experiment and all stage durations can be varied with this granularity without
requiring to run new simulations.

Furthermore, various combinations of stage durations can be chosen to make many ex-
periment cycles. This work focuses on varying one particular stage duration, the MT clean-
ing stage. All other stage durations are kept constant and set close to recommendations from
a previous publication [2]. Table 4.1 shows simulated stage durations that were arbitrarily
chosen and optimum durations that were chosen to simplify and reduce the optimization
routine to just varying the MT cleaning stage time.

To measure the exponential time constant of the neutron beta decay, two durations have
to be chosen for the magnetic storage period from Eq. 1.10. 20 s and 1550 s were adopted
following [13].

Simulation Stages and Key Analyses

UCN energy distribution histograms for both high-field seeking and low-field seeking neu-
trons from simulations were used to track UCNs through a PENeLOPE experiment cycle.
In the following, I provide a summary of the main objectives of each simulated stage as I
discuss them in Section 4.2.1 in further detail.
1. Filling Stage

• Objective: Normalize energy distributions of LFSs and HFSs based on the UCN
source flux at FRM II. The source fills neutrons into the storage volume of PENe-
LOPE. Pre-polarization is done between source and storage volume to reduce the
number of HFSs in PENeLOPE during filling.

• Stage is used to explain: LFS energy distributions are used to explain the nor-
malization process, which involves scaling the simulated production rate to the UCN
source flux using Equation 4.8. Although not shown, HFS distributions are normalized
through the same process.

2. Marginally Trapped (MT) Cleaning

• Objective: Remove UCNs from the storage volume that cannot be fully magnetically
stored, and which are prone to losses due to wall interactions.

• Stage is used to explain: The energy distributions of subsequent stages must be
connected to the filling stage, maintaining normalization relative to the UCN source, to
accurately track UCNs through the energy distributions across an entire PENeLOPE
cycle. As the spectrum progresses, it evolves due to effects introduced at each stage.

55



To account for this, the connection is established by calculating survival probability
distributions for each stage, which are then adjusted—both scaled and shaped—using
the experiment distribution from the preceding stage.

• Main Observations: Higher energy UCNs are effectively removed if the spin flip
probability of the storage walls is low enough.

3. Ramp-up Stage

• Objective: Turn on main magnetic field to transition from material storage in PENe-
LOPE to magnetic storage.

• Stage is used to explain: The LFS and HFS energy shift distributions are used to
observe the shifts caused by the magnetic field. Simulations that start with only LFSs
or only HFSs are created for all stages with a magnetic field to separate spin-flipped
UCN into additional energy distributions. This distinction ensures a comprehensive
understanding of how the magnetic field influences energy dynamics.

• Main Observations: High-field seekers lose energy, low-field seekers gain energy.

4. HFS Cleaning (Stages A & B)

• Objective: Remove HFSs via lowering of absorber rings.

• Stage is used to explain: HFS energy distributions are plotted to visualize the
removal of HFSs using absorber rings. Special attention is given to empty bins in
the energy distribution, as low statistics may lead to inaccuracies. Another approach
estimates the experimental distributions for these stages by utilizing calculated storage
lifetimes to determine the distributions.

Since the simulations with the magnetic field turned on start with either HFSs or
LFSs, this allows for observations on the impact of first-order spin flips to second-
order spin flips on the ratio of HFSs to LFSs stored in PENeLOPE. The production
of HFSs from spinflips is estimated for each simulation with different βSS.

5. Storage Stage

• Objective: To store LFSs with total energies under the magneto-gravitational po-
tential 115 neV for a short storage time of t1 = 20 s and a long storage time of
t2 = 1550 s.

• Stage is used to explain: The analysis focuses on the impact of marginally trapped
UCNs (MT UCNs) during this stage, evaluating how their losses during wall interac-
tions affect the neutron lifetime. However, the inclusion of β-decay in the simulations
introduces significant uncertainties, primarily due to low statistics. These uncertain-
ties could overshadow the effect of MT UCN losses on the neutron lifetime, making

56



it challenging to isolate and accurately assess their specific contribution. To get past
this issue, a filtering process is applied to exclude UCNs that undergo β−decay in the
simulations. This way, LFS energy distributions would only be dependent on other
loss mechanisms other than β−decay.

• Main Observations: UCN losses that occur during this stage contribute to a shift
of the measured neutron lifetime. Energy distributions are dependent on the value of
βSS . Low statistics in simulations makes β−decay have a high statistical uncertainty.

6. Ramp-Down and Counting Stage

• Objective: Magnetic field is turned off, LFSs and HFSs are counted.

• Stage is used to explain: The β−decay filtering applied in the storage stage is
corrected to account for the decay effects in the final combined energy distribution.
The ramp-down and counting stage’s energy distribution is connected with the storage
stage to obtain the final experiment distribution at the end of the PENeLOPE cycle.
The connection is done by applying the effect of this stage to the storage stage’s
experiment distribution. The collection efficiency is calculated for simulations with
each βSS .

As discussed in Section 1.2, UCNs that interact with material walls may undergo reflection,

be specularly or diffusely transmitted into the material. For transmission, the refraction
rules of neutron optics are applied. The left side of Figure 4.1 illustrates specular reflection.
